# Claim adjudication table

Every claim below was checked against the cited evidence. `Partially supported`
means a kernel of truth exists but the claim as commonly stated overstates it.

| # | Claim | Verdict | What the evidence shows | Sources |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Vitamin D prevents fractures in healthy adults | **Unsupported** | The largest trials in people not selected for deficiency found no reduction in total, hip or non-vertebral fractures regardless of baseline 25(OH)D. | R06, R21 |
| 2 | Calcium plus vitamin D prevents hip fractures in frail or deficient older people | **Partially supported** | Pooled trials show about a 16% relative reduction in hip fracture, driven by institutionalised and deficient populations; vitamin D alone does not reduce fracture. | R19, R20 |
| 3 | Vitamin D prevents falls | **Partially supported** | 800-1000 IU per day is associated with fewer falls, but doses above 1000 IU per day and bolus dosing are associated with more; the USPSTF recommends against supplementation for fall prevention. | R61, R18 |
| 4 | Vitamin D prevents colds and flu | **Partially supported** | An individual-participant meta-analysis found a modest reduction in acute respiratory infection with daily dosing, but the larger 2025 aggregate analysis was null with evidence of publication bias. | R13, R14 |
| 5 | Vitamin D prevents COVID-19 | **Unsupported** | No trial has shown a reliable reduction in infection or severe disease, and the largest synthesis of respiratory infection trials is null overall. | R14, R22 |
| 6 | Vitamin D prevents cancer | **Unsupported** | VITAL found no reduction in invasive cancer incidence over 5.3 years. | R05, R16 |
| 7 | Vitamin D reduces cancer deaths | **Partially supported** | Pooled trials show about a 13-15% relative reduction in cancer mortality, mainly with daily dosing; the absolute benefit is small. | R16, R15 |
| 8 | Vitamin D prevents heart attacks and strokes | **Unsupported** | VITAL found no reduction in major cardiovascular events; D-Health showed only a non-significant trend. | R05, R11 |
| 9 | Vitamin D prevents autoimmune disease | **Partially supported** | VITAL found a 22% reduction during treatment, but the effect was no longer present after supplementation stopped. | R07, R08 |
| 10 | Vitamin D prevents type 2 diabetes | **Partially supported** | The D2d trial was null, but pooled trial data in high-risk prediabetes show about 15% less progression. | R12, R04 |
| 11 | Everyone should aim for 25(OH)D of 30 ng/mL or higher | **Unsupported** | No trial establishes an outcome-based threshold, and the 2024 Endocrine Society guideline dropped the 30 ng/mL target. | R02, R64 |
| 12 | Everyone should have their vitamin D level tested | **Unsupported** | The 2024 guideline suggests against routine screening and against follow-up testing to guide dosing in general-population groups. | R02 |
| 13 | Vitamin D toxicity is common | **False** | Toxicity is rare below 150 ng/mL and almost always follows sustained intakes above 10 000 IU per day. | R40, R54 |
| 14 | 10 000 IU per day is dangerous | **Partially supported** | Three years at 10 000 IU caused mild hypercalcemia in 9% of participants, all reversible, with no difference in clinical adverse events. | R54, R52 |
| 15 | Vitamin D causes kidney stones | **Partially supported** | Vitamin D alone at moderate or high intermittent doses did not increase stones; the signal comes from calcium co-supplementation. | R53, R40 |
| 16 | 5000 IU is a sensible universal dose | **Unsupported** | Most adults meet requirements at 600-800 IU, and 5000 IU exceeds the tolerable upper limit; it is a correction dose for documented deficiency, not a default. | R02, R52 |
| 17 | Vitamin D3 is better than vitamin D2 | **Supported** | D3 produces roughly 40% greater increases in total 25(OH)D than D2 at the same daily dose. | R43 |
| 18 | Take vitamin D with a fatty meal | **Supported** | Fat increases peak absorption by about 32%, although the effect on 25(OH)D after 90 days was not significant in one trial. | R41, R42 |
| 19 | Sprays and sublingual drops are absorbed better than capsules | **Unsupported** | No controlled comparison shows a superior 25(OH)D response, and fat co-ingestion is the only consistently demonstrated modifier. | R41, R42 |
| 20 | Vitamin K2 prevents osteoporosis and fractures | **Partially supported** | Some MK-7 and MK-4 trials show slower bone loss or fewer fractures, but the best-powered MK-7 trial found no BMD benefit and meta-analyses are inconsistent. | R23, R26, R24 |
| 21 | Vitamin K2 removes calcium from your arteries | **Unsupported** | K2 activates matrix Gla protein, but trials show no consistent reduction in calcification and no clinical outcome benefit. | R30, R36 |
| 22 | Vitamin K2 slows vascular calcification | **Partially supported** | Pooled trials show a small reduction in coronary calcium score, but the largest dedicated trials were neutral and none was powered for events. | R36, R31 |
| 23 | D3 plus K2 works better than D3 alone | **Unsupported** | No trial shows an advantage for hard outcomes; the one positive BMD trial used an activated vitamin D analogue, and better-powered trials found no added bone benefit. | R28, R24, R25 |
| 24 | MK-7 is better than MK-4 | **Partially supported** | MK-7 has a much longer half-life and better bioavailability, but head-to-head outcome trials do not exist. | R44, R59 |
| 25 | Vitamin K2 is safe for everyone | **Partially supported** | No upper limit has been set and trials up to 999 mcg are clean, but K2 is contraindicated with vitamin K antagonists. | R38, R37 |
| 26 | Vitamin K2 is safe with warfarin | **False** | MK-7 at 45 mcg per day lowered INR by 20-37% in a controlled study, and doses as low as 10 mcg were judged clinically relevant in some people. | R37, R39 |
| 27 | Vitamin K2 is safe with apixaban or rivaroxaban | **Partially supported** | Direct oral anticoagulants do not depend on vitamin K, so no mechanism exists, but no trial has tested co-administration. | R39, R37 |
| 28 | Supplements are unregulated so none can be trusted | **Partially supported** | Label accuracy varies widely, but most products meet claims and certified products perform better. | R48, R46, R47 |
| 29 | A USP or NSF seal proves the supplement works | **False** | Certification verifies identity, potency and contaminants, not efficacy. | R50, R51 |
| 30 | Natto and fermented foods supply enough K2 | **Partially supported** | Natto is the richest dietary source, but intake is highly variable and dietary K2 has not been shown to change clinical outcomes. | R39, R59 |
| 31 | Vitamin D strengthens bones in everyone | **Partially supported** | It prevents rickets and osteomalacia and helps deficient or institutionalised people, but does not increase bone density or prevent fractures in replete adults. | R06, R19 |
| 32 | Vitamin D supplements are a substitute for sunlight and a healthy diet | **Unsupported** | Supplements correct a specific nutrient gap; they do not reproduce other effects of sun exposure or replace dietary patterns. | R40, R55 |
| 33 | Higher vitamin D doses give better results | **False** | Above about 1000 IU per day for falls, and above 4000 IU for safety, higher doses are associated with more harm and no extra benefit. | R52, R61 |
| 34 | Vitamin D should be stopped in kidney disease | **Partially supported** | Supplementation is often appropriate but requires monitoring because impaired kidneys handle calcium and phosphate differently. | R40, R54 |
